candidate_sources.title: Mango anthracnose (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides)
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet from University of Hawaii CTAHR covering mango anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, including symptoms on leaves, fruits, twigs, and flowers, and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Mango anthracnose (009) - Lucid Apps
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated fact sheet on mango anthracnose covering symptoms on leaves (irregular necrotic lesions with chlorotic haloes), fruits (dark brown to black decay patches), twigs, and flowers, plus pathogen details and management.

candidate_sources.title: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides (anthracnose) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, the primary causal agent of mango anthracnose, covering host range, symptoms, epidemiology, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Black Spot (BBS) of Mango in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae causes bacterial black spot (bacterial canker) and is a major mango pathogen in tropical and subtropical areas. The bacterium induces raised, angular, black leaf lesions, sometimes with a yellow chlorotic halo. Severe infections cause defoliation and/or premature fruit drop. Fruit symptoms first appear as small water-soaked spots on the lenticels turning into star-shaped, erumpent lesions which exude an infectious gum.

candidate_sources.title: Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae (mango black spot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. mangiferaeindicae, the causal agent of mango black spot (bacterial canker). Covers host range, distribution, symptoms on leaves, fruit and twigs, epidemiology, and management including copper bactericides and cultural control measures.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Canker of Mango, Mangifera indica, Caused by Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae, Confirmed for the First Time in the Americas | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial canker of mango caused by Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae confirmed for the first time in the Americas. Symptoms include angular black lesions on leaves with yellow halos, twig cankers, and star-shaped erumpent lesions on fruit exuding gum. Pathogen identity confirmed via pathogenicity tests and molecular characterisation.

candidate_sources.title: Deporaus marginatus (mango leaf-cutting weevil)
candidate_sources.snippet: The most obvious symptoms of attack by the mango leaf-cutting weevil are young leaves that are cut and fallen to the ground, with stripped shoots easily visible on infested plants. Adult feeding produces 'windowpanes' on young leaves. The main damage is produced by female weevils, which cut young leaves, and infested shoots become almost leafless. Damage to autumn shoots has a great impact on fruit setting and yield, with the rate of barren shoots potentially exceeding 80% if control measures are not taken.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf-cutting Weevil | Pests & Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Distinctive damage symptoms include young leaf bits below the tree and stripped shoots visible from a distance. Adult feeding produces 'windowpanes' on young leaves. The adult female deposits eggs on the upper surface of a young leaf near the midrib and then severs the leaf near the stalk, whereupon it falls to the ground. Damage to young shoots impacts fruit setting and yield.

candidate_sources.title: Susceptibility of Different Varieties of Mango to Leaf Cutting Weevil, Deporaus marginatus P. and its Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Study of susceptibility of different mango varieties to Deporaus marginatus and evaluation of control measures. Insecticides such as trichlorphon, deltamethrin and fenvalerate are effective for control when applied when young leaves are 3 cm wide. Cultural control includes collection and burning of cut leaves, and ploughing soil under crowns to kill pupae.

candidate_sources.title: Mango Dieback Disease | Pests & Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Disease symptoms of dieback on mango are commonly associated with drying and withering of twigs from top downwards, followed by discoloration, drying and eventual dropping of leaves. When the fungus attacks the leaves, their margins roll upwards turning them a brownish colour, and later a scorch-like appearance develops, followed by the dropping of the infected leaves. The pathogenic fungus Lasiodiplodia theobromae has been identified as the causal agent.

candidate_sources.title: Detection and Management of Mango Dieback Disease in the United Arab Emirates - PMC
candidate_sources.snippet: Mango dieback disease caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae is considered the most destructive disease, leading to significant yield loss and low fruit quality of mango. Symptoms include general wilting of mango trees, dieback of twigs, curling and drying of leaves, complete defoliation and discolouration of vascular regions of stems and branches. Systemic fungicides significantly inhibited mycelial growth of L. theobromae.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Lasiodiplodia theobromae Causing Dieback, a Destructive Disease on Mango Trees, in Saudi Arabia | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Lasiodiplodia theobromae causing dieback, a destructive disease on mango trees. Dieback symptoms include drying and withering of twigs from top downwards, discoloration and dropping of leaves, leaf margins rolling upwards turning brownish, scorch-like appearance, and eventual death of affected trees. First report from Saudi Arabia.

candidate_sources.title: Erosomyia mangiferae (mango gall midge)
candidate_sources.snippet: Females lay eggs singly into the tissue of young leaves on the under surface, leaving a small reddish spot. Gall formation begins within seven days and attains a maximum diameter of about 3-4 mm. Heavily galled leaves curl up and drop off prematurely, causing dieback of whole branches in susceptible cultivars. Synonyms include Dasineura mangiferae, Erosomyia indica, Mangodiplosis mangiferae, and Procystiphora mangiferae.

candidate_sources.title: Erosomyia mangiferae (mango gall midge)
candidate_sources.snippet: Infested parts become covered with many small, raised galls or blisters on leaves, buds, inflorescences and young fruits. Serious outbreaks result in defoliation and reduced fruit yield. Adult midges are small flies about 1-2 mm long. Includes cultural, mechanical, and chemical control methods.

candidate_sources.title: How To Control Mango Gall Midge And All You Need To Know | Greenlife
candidate_sources.snippet: Mango gall midge (Erosomyia mangiferae) causes small raised galls or blisters on young mango leaves. Heavily infested leaves curl and drop prematurely. Management includes cultural controls and chemical treatments. Covers symptoms, biology, and integrated pest management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Mango Powdery Mildew
candidate_sources.snippet: Official University of Hawaii CTAHR extension factsheet (PD-46) on mango powdery mildew. Covers symptoms (whitish-gray haze on panicles, white spores on young leaves and flowers, infected fruits remain small and deformed), pathogen (Oidium mangiferae, ectophytic and biotrophic), environmental conditions for disease development, and management options.

candidate_sources.title: Oidium mangiferae (powdery mildew of mango) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Oidium mangiferae, the causal agent of mango powdery mildew. A serious disease causing 20-90% crop losses mainly due to blossom infection. Covers taxonomy, distribution, symptoms, biology, epidemiology, and management including sulfur/copper fungicides and biocontrol with Ampelomyces quisqualis.

candidate_sources.title: Oidium mangiferae (powdery mildew of mango) | PlantWise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: PlantWise Plus (CABI) knowledge bank entry for Oidium mangiferae covering identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, natural enemies, cultural and chemical control. White powdery growth on leaves, flowers, and young fruits; conidia germinate between 9-30.5°C optimal at 22°C; disease severity inversely related to sunshine hours.

candidate_sources.title: Mango Tree Sooty Mold - UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County
candidate_sources.snippet: Sooty mold fungi grow on the sugars left by insects on the foliage, turning the leaf surface black. In severe cases, trees turn completely black due to the mould over the entire surface of twigs and leaves. Control involves eliminating the sugary food supply by controlling sap-feeding insects (aphids, whiteflies, scales) on the foliage.

candidate_sources.title: Capnodium mangiferae (sooty mould of mango) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Capnodium mangiferae, the causal agent of sooty mould of mango. Covers identity, distribution, hosts/species affected, symptoms, and further information. Capnodium mangiferae is a facultative saprophytic fungus belonging to Family Capnodiaceae, Order Capnodiales, Phylum Ascomycota, producing a black powdery mass of chain spores on the plant surface.

candidate_sources.title: Sooty moulds (051) - Lucid Apps (Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds)
candidate_sources.snippet: Black moulds grow on honeydew discharged by sap-sucking insects (aphids, planthoppers, whiteflies, scales) onto leaves and fruits. The fungi do not infect the leaves but shut out sunlight, weakening growth, causing leaves to die early, and reducing fruit quality. Covers symptoms, pathogen identity, and management for sooty moulds on mango and other crops.
